author: spatialnasir
text:
I uninstalled VS Code. Twice.

Some of my GitHub repos were hit by PolinRider, a supply chain attack that spreads through compromised npm packages.

It drops obfuscated JavaScript into your project, then injects a hidden task into .vscode/tasks.json that runs the moment you open the folder in VS Code or any fork like Cursor.

I ran the PolinRider cleanup script from OpenSourceMalware, cleaned my repos and removed VS Code. Everything looked clean.

Then I reinstalled VS Code, and strange activity from my machine showed up in my GitHub security logs again.

So VS Code went for good, and I switched to Zed. I was wary of its agent features since I'm not a vibe-coder, but so far I'm not going back. It opens from the CLI in 1.249s, it's minimal and customizable, and its plugin ecosystem is growing.

PS: If you use VS Code or a fork, check your projects for unexpected .vscode/tasks.json files. If you find one, rotate your GitHub tokens and SSH keys.

author: psoheil
text:
Microsoft’s AI Agent Framework was compromised through a Python supply-chain attack.

Two malicious versions of Microsoft’s official agent-framework package (1.26.1 and 1.26.2) were uploaded to PyPI, distributing malware designed to steal developer and cloud credentials.

What makes this particularly concerning:

• No import required: A malicious Python .pth startup hook executes automatically whenever Python starts.

• Credential harvesting: The malware searches environment variables, configuration files, Git credentials, Docker credentials, and application secrets.

• Cloud identity theft: It actively requests authentication tokens from Azure Managed Identity, Azure DevOps, and GitHub Actions.

• CI/CD exposure: Build agents and automated deployment environments could expose privileged credentials and enterprise infrastructure.

• Trusted publisher compromised: This wasn’t a typosquatting attack. Malicious releases came through Microsoft’s legitimate publishing channel.

The bigger concern here is the trust we place in our software dependencies.

A package doesn’t need to be malicious when we first adopt it. A compromised publisher can turn a trusted dependency into an attack vector overnight.

For organizations building AI agents and integrating cloud services, dependency security needs to be treated as part of the application security strategy, not just a development hygiene issue.

My takeaway: Locking dependencies, scanning packages, isolating build environments, and limiting credential permissions are no longer optional security practices.

#CyberSecurity #SupplyChainSecurity #Python #Microsoft #AIAgents #DevSecOps #CloudSecurity #Azure

author: NedPeterson99
text:
Leaked credentials. A 22-hour window. Every secret in the cluster readable, and the console you'd use to rotate them was down.

Rackspace told customers that on Nov. 17, from about 00:20 to 22:00 UTC, an unauthorized party used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot, its Kubernetes platform. Acting as legitimate users in some customer organizations, the attacker could create pods, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes. Rackspace learned of it on Nov. 18 from a customer report, then revoked tokens and sessions, removed the unauthorized pods and rotated keys. The Spot admin console went offline for the cleanup, so customers could not manage clusters or rotate their own credentials until service was fully restored on Nov. 21. Customers are told to reissue Spot API tokens, replace refresh tokens in automation, pull fresh kubeconfig files, rotate every credential stored in cluster Secrets, and review logs on connected services back to Nov. 17.

The lesson for CISOs: a Kubernetes Secret is only as private as the least-protected account that can read it, and one leaked platform credential turns a tenant's secrets store into a key ring for every database, registry and cloud account it unlocks. Keep high-value secrets in an external vault with short-lived leases, scope RBAC so no identity can list Secrets cluster-wide, and rehearse rotation on the assumption that your provider's console is unavailable when you need it most.

https://t.co/1Vtu4yIn0u

#CloudSecurity #Kubernetes #CyberSecurity

author: Sujeet
text:
Rackspace told customers that attackers used leaked credentials to get into its Spot cloud platform on November 17, between about 00:20 and 22:00 UTC, and in some customer organizations they could act as legitimate users — creating pods in Kubernetes clusters, reading Kubernetes Secrets, and listing nodes and volumes. Secrets hold the passwords, tokens, and API keys your applications use to reach databases and cloud services. Rackspace learned of it on November 18, from a customer report. It revoked tokens and sessions, removed the unauthorized pods, rotated keys, and told affected customers to reissue API tokens, replace refresh tokens, download fresh kubeconfigs, and rotate every stored secret. The admin console stayed down for days while the platform was secured; service was fully restored November 21.

The part that stays with me is the shape of it: one leaked credential, and the blast radius is every secret in every cluster it could reach. A managed platform turns a single identity compromise into an infrastructure-wide exposure, and the customers couldn't even rotate their credentials while the console was down.

A leaked credential is never just a login. In a managed platform, it's the keys to everyone else's house too.

author: valuecm
text:
If your AI agents run in a Python environment that also holds your cloud keys, last week's agent-framework compromise is the incident to read.

On 17 November, Wiz says, two malicious versions of Microsoft's agent-framework package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published to PyPI. Both were gone within about an hour, but the package gets around 41,000 downloads a week. They dropped a .pth file into site-packages, and Python runs .pth files every time the interpreter starts, so the stealer ran even if nothing imported agent-framework. It went after environment variables with names containing TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB and OPENAI, among others. Wiz says the attacker appears to have used a stolen client certificate for Microsoft's own release pipeline, and the attacker's tooling identified itself as Cairn, an open-source AI penetration-testing framework. Separately, Amazon reported on 20 November that a China-linked group's Cairn agents found and exploited a zero-day on their own.

What I would do: pin agent libraries to exact versions with hashes and upgrade on purpose, never through a floating version in CI. Don't keep long-lived keys in the environment where agents and their dependencies run. If 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 ever landed anywhere, the advisories say to rebuild from a clean environment and rotate every credential that machine could reach. 1.26.0 is the last safe version.

#threatreport:
ARTEX is a publicly available, AI-assisted penetration-testing framework that operators run from their own servers. A planner converts an operator’s goal into attack tasks, while worker agents use tools such as Nmap, curl and Impacket, share findings through common graphs and a blackboard, and record traffic. It can switch between AI providers and ingest reconnaissance data. ARTEX is not malware installed on a victim; its use is associated with activity across identity, web, cloud and endpoint environments.

Reported attack behavior includes rapidly retrieving JavaScript source maps, runtime configuration and API documentation, then using discovered routes for further probing. Agents test nonexistent paths, manipulate OAuth callbacks, attempt unsigned tokens, spray passwords against Entra ID and Okta, and abuse account recovery or open registration. After gaining access, they may explore Microsoft Graph, add application credentials or assign roles, read Azure Key Vault secrets, enumerate AWS services, and search CloudWatch logs for sensitive information. Activity can adapt to rate limits by changing endpoints or source addresses and may continue for 24–30 hours.

Inside networks, activity often appears as short bursts of tool use separated by long pauses. Agents may try multiple remote-access methods, including SSH, RDP, PsExec, WinRM and other tools, and may create web shells, files, accounts, scheduled tasks or persistence mechanisms. Reported artifacts include files with “artex” or “artx” in their names and remote-access tools such as WISP, Vshell and AdaptixC2. Some campaigns involved human operators providing instructions at decision points.

Multiple actors have reportedly used ARTEX, including Storm-0940, Storm-3358 and VAPOR PANDA; its use is not, by itself, evidence of a specific actor. The European Commission confirmed an AI-driven campaign that disrupted applications but did not publicly attribute it or confirm ARTEX use. Reports also describe exposed ARTEX consoles, sometimes hosted alongside other attack tools.

Useful detection patterns include regular password failures across many accounts, application credential or role changes initiated by service principals, unusual Graph or cloud discovery activity, source-map retrieval followed by undocumented API calls, and several unrelated user-agent families from one source in a short period. Endpoint hunting should look for web or database services launching shells or download tools, scripts written to web directories, unusual outbound connections, and lateral movement across many hosts. ARTEX has no associated CVE; reported intrusions exploit existing weaknesses such as weak passwords, exposed configuration, stolen credentials and excessive permissions.
